title: Modern Stoicism, carefully
hook: online Stoicism can drift into toughness and money; the originals aimed at virtue and kindness

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was cognitive therapy, an old Stoic idea inside modern therapy rooms. Your line was examine the thought.

Scroll for a minute and you'll find it. A marble bust of Marcus Aurelius, lit dramatically, over a caption about cold showers, never showing weakness and crushing your competition. A video promising Stoic secrets to a seven-figure income. A man in a gym explaining that real Stoics don't cry. Some of it is harmless. Some of it is useful. But set beside the Stoics you've read this year, some of it sounds like a different school wearing their clothes.
screen: `A MARBLE BUST AND A COLD SHOWER.` → `STOIC SECRETS TO WEALTH.` → `A DIFFERENT SCHOOL IN THEIR CLOTHES?`

segments.voice: First, two spellings. Small-s stoic, in everyday English, means someone who endures without showing feeling. Capital-S Stoic means a member of the school of the painted porch. The two overlap a little and get confused a lot. Second, the aim. For Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, the only true good was virtue: wisdom, justice, courage and self-control, lived out with other people. Money, status, even health were, in their language, indifferent: fine to have, fine to use well, never the point. A Stoic route to riches would have puzzled them. Seneca was rich, and he spent letters warning himself not to be owned by it. Third, toughness. Endurance mattered to the Stoics, but not coldness. Epictetus tells his students he shouldn't be unfeeling like a statue; he should keep his relationships as a son, a brother, a citizen. Marcus reminds himself again and again to be gentle and patient with people who annoy him, and calls kindness hard to defeat when it's real. Fourth, reading the modern stuff. Not with a sneer: some people find real help in it, and some modern writers handle the sources well. Just with one question. Does this slogan point toward being a better neighbor, more just, more honest, kinder? Or only toward being harder to hurt and better at winning? If it's only the second, check the source. The originals rarely stop there.
screen: `SMALL-S STOIC, CAPITAL-S STOIC.` · `THE AIM: VIRTUE, NOT RICHES.` · `NOT UNFEELING LIKE A STATUE.` · `CHECK THE SLOGAN AGAINST THE SOURCE.` · then, large: `VIRTUE, NOT TOUGHNESS.`

segments.voice: Think of one Stoic-sounding slogan you've heard, maybe control what you can, or don't let them see you sweat, and hold it beside what you've read this year. Where does it match the old teachers, and where does it leave something out, like kindness, justice or other people? Without judging whoever shared it, notice what's missing, and what you'd add back.
Modern Stoicism: the old school's revival today, best read carefully, with the original aim in view, which was virtue and kindness, not toughness and money. Today's word.
Your line: virtue, not toughness. The old Stoics aimed at kindness, never coldness. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often test popular Stoic slogans against the ancient texts, asking whether they point toward virtue and care for others or only toward endurance and success.

chat.says: Isn't Stoicism basically about being tough, hiding your feelings, and getting rich?
options: Not really; the old Stoics aimed at virtue and kindness, and money was never the point.
Yes; the Stoics taught that real strength means feeling nothing, like a statue.
Mostly; Seneca was rich, so the school taught wealth as the reward of discipline.
chat.meaning: For the Stoics the only true good was virtue. Epictetus said not to be unfeeling like a statue, and money was never the point.

Marcus Aurelius.meaning: a Roman emperor whose private notebook became the Meditations

Zeno.meaning: the founder of the Stoic school

Seneca.meaning: a rich Roman Stoic who wrote letters on living well

painted porch.meaning: the colonnade in Athens where the Stoic school began
